answer: From Maxwell's equations in free space ($\rho = 0$, $\mathbf{J} = 0$), taking the curl of Faraday's law and substituting Ampere-Maxwell's law yields the wave equation:$$\nabla^2 \mathbf{E} = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}$$Comparing this with the standard wave equation $\nabla^2 \mathbf{E} = \frac{1}{v^2} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}$, the velocity of the electromagnetic wave is:$$v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}}$$Substituting the values of permeability of free space $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{H/m}$ and permittivity $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{F/m}$:$$v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times (8.854 \times 10^{-12})}} = 3 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s} = c$$Thus, the velocity of an electromagnetic wave in free space equals the velocity of light.
proTip: Remember to explicitly substitute the numerical values of $\mu_0$ and $\varepsilon_0$ to show it equals $c$.
